top.headline: Miami Cargo Crash Raises Concerns About the Airline Flying for Amazon
top.blurb: A 21 Air cargo jet flying for Amazon overshot the runway in Miami and caught fire after one pilot warned the other the plane was coming in too fast. Former pilots and a departing safety director had raised alarms about the carrier for years, and the crew flying it had comparatively little experience on the Boeing 767.

top.headline: Centrists Are Soft-Launching the Idea That We Have a Little Too Much Democracy
top.blurb: A wave of centrist-liberal commentary is arguing that small-dollar donors and mass participation have made the Democratic Party too responsive to its base, echoing a distaste for wide participation once associated mainly with the right. The Intercept traces the funding behind groups pushing the party back toward a wealthier, more centralized donor class.

top.headline: Telangana SIR: Activists Flag Vague Notices, Seek Transparency in Hearings
top.blurb: Civil society groups told Telangana's chief electoral officer that Special Intensive Revision notices give voters only vague reasons like "not mapped" or "name mismatched," with no way to check a case's status. They want written, itemised reasons for every notice and daily public tallies of hearings and outcomes constituency by constituency.

top.headline: Why Has India's G20 Fanfare Not Been Replicated for the BRICS Summit?
top.blurb: Where India's 2023 G20 presidency came with a nationwide "People's Presidency" campaign turning diplomacy into political theatre, this year's BRICS summit in Delhi has drawn comparatively little pageantry. Scroll.in argues the gap reflects a harder geopolitical moment — strained US ties, the Middle East war and an unresolved China border dispute — that leaves less room for triumphant messaging.

top.headline: Houthis Advance on Yemeni Government Strongholds of Marib and Taiz
top.blurb: Houthi fighters are pushing toward the oil-and-gas-rich province of Marib and the city of Taiz as Saudi-backed government forces respond with air strikes, with more than 900 people killed or injured and thousands of families displaced in under a week. Analysts say a split government command across rival armies is hampering any unified response to the fast-moving offensive.

top.headline: BRICS Summit 2026: What Are the Key Takeaways?
top.blurb: Leaders at the Delhi summit unanimously adopted a New Delhi Declaration calling for restraint in the Middle East and criticising the global trade war, but stopped short of naming the US or condemning either the US-Israeli strikes on Iran or Iran's own strikes on Gulf states. The bloc leaned on vaguer language precisely where its members disagree most, from Ukraine to Gaza.

top.headline: India Cruise to a Record-Extending Eighth Women's Asia Cup Title
top.blurb: Shafali Verma's 24-ball fifty, the fastest in Women's T20 Asia Cup history, anchored a 129-run opening stand with Smriti Mandhana as India posted 183 for 5 in Dubai. Sri Lanka never recovered, bowled out for 111 by Deepti Sharma and Shree Charani's spin, handing India a 72-run win and their eighth Asia Cup title.

top.headline: 'Call My Agent! The Movie' Brings Back the Charm of the Original Show
top.blurb: Scroll.in's review of the film sequel to the beloved French series finds that creator Fanny Herrero recaptures the show's blend of talent-agency chaos and messy personal lives, leaning on Camille Cottin and Laure Calamy to carry it. Cameos including George Clooney sportingly enduring a joke at his own expense add to a movie that mostly rewards viewers who already know the agents.

bengal.headline: West Bengal Census: Fearing Welfare Cuts, Households Undercount Assets
bengal.blurb: As West Bengal's house-listing census phase wraps up, enumerators say many households are deliberately understating assets and income for fear that an accurate count could cost them welfare-scheme eligibility, with some residents reportedly resisting enumeration altogether.

travel.headline: Best Places to Visit in Japan in 2026: 15 Destinations for Every Type of Traveler
travel.blurb: Lonely Planet's roster ranges from Tokyo's megacity buzz to the beaches of Okinawa and the mountain views around Fuji, aimed at first-timers, repeat visitors and travelers chasing something further off the beaten path alike.

travel.headline: Mozambique Protects Mount Mabu, a Hotspot of More Than 200 Butterfly Species
travel.blurb: Mozambique has formally protected Mount Mabu's forests as a 9,341-hectare Community Conservation Area, home to more than 200 butterfly species and dozens of species discovered there since 2005. Stewardship goes to the local communities who have treated the forest as sacred and kept it standing for generations, rather than to a central park authority.

happy.headline: How Did the Nation Get Its Name? Other Suggestions Included Columbia and the United States of Alleghania
happy.blurb: Congress settled on "United States of America" 250 years ago this month, but the name stayed contested for decades afterward: Washington Irving proposed honoring the Appalachians in 1839, Edgar Allan Poe seconded him, and an 1845 historical society committee formally recommended "Republic of Allegania" instead.

tech_top.headline: Asian AI Stocks Slide as Anthropic, OpenAI and Musk Call for Slower Development
tech_top.pm_note: When the labs setting the pace openly call for slowing down and markets punish their own suppliers for it, 'ship fast' stops being a costless default in your own roadmap conversations.
tech_top.blurb: SoftBank fell as much as 13% in Tokyo and chipmakers Kioxia, SK Hynix and Samsung all dropped sharply after Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk each backed calls over the weekend to deliberately pace frontier AI development. The selloff hit AI-infrastructure suppliers hardest, a sign investors are pricing a slowdown as a real possibility rather than posturing.

tech_top.headline: Altman Says OpenAI Won't Wait for Legislation to Pace AI Development
tech_top.pm_note: OpenAI is separately asking Congress whether coordinating a slowdown with rivals could violate antitrust law — a reminder that 'let's all agree to go slower' is legally fraught between competitors, not just a safety talking point.
tech_top.blurb: Sam Altman said OpenAI "welcomes a federal framework" for AI safety but does not believe the industry needs to wait for legislation or an antitrust exemption to start building confidence with outside auditors. The comments follow reports that OpenAI has quietly asked lawmakers whether a coordinated industry slowdown could run afoul of the Sherman Antitrust Act.

tech_top.headline: Anthropic Expects a Second Straight Profitable Quarter Ahead of Its IPO
tech_top.pm_note: Anthropic is using an old-economy metric — actual operating profit — to make its case to IPO investors, at a moment when most AI labs are still selling growth alone.
tech_top.blurb: Anthropic told prospective investors it expects positive adjusted operating income for a second consecutive quarter, with gross margins above 80% before revenue-sharing and training costs. The company posted over $11.5 billion in second-quarter revenue, a 14-fold jump from a year earlier, as it prepares an IPO aiming to rival SpaceX's record $86.3 billion offering.

tech_101.text: A voluntary, industry-wide slowdown in how fast AI labs release more capable models — as opposed to a government-imposed pause — meant to leave more time for safety work without any one company falling behind.

A profitability measure that strips out one-time or non-cash costs to show whether a business's core operations are actually in the black — the number Anthropic is highlighting to IPO investors instead of raw revenue growth.

science.headline: Blue Light Breaks a Long-Standing Chemistry Rule, Unlocking 3D Drug Building Blocks
science.blurb: University of Bristol chemists used blue-light photocatalysis to make nitrogen-containing molecules cyclize in a pattern that overrides the decades-old "rule-of-five" governing such reactions. The method produces rigid, three-dimensional molecular scaffolds that could replace the flat aromatic rings drugmakers have long relied on, which often fit poorly into 3D biological targets.

science.headline: ESA Launches Sentinel-3C and FLEX to Watch Earth's Oceans and Plant Life
science.blurb: A Vega-C rocket is set to carry the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite and the FLEX mission into orbit together from French Guiana, with Sentinel-3C joining two earlier satellites to monitor oceans, land, ice and atmosphere. FLEX carries a first-of-its-kind instrument that detects the faint fluorescent glow plants emit during photosynthesis, offering a direct read on vegetation health worldwide.

science.headline: Global Warming Is Breaking a 400-Year Climate Link Between Two Oceans
science.blurb: Paleoclimate records show the Indian and Pacific Oceans' atmospheric circulations stayed coupled for most of the last 400 years, interrupted only briefly by 19th-century volcanic eruptions. Woods Hole researchers found that human-caused warming has now driven an exceptional, sustained breakdown in that coupling since the 1980s, with no precedent in the historical record.

philosophy.headline: Democracy and Liberalism Are Incompatible
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Tongdong Bai argues that majority rule and liberal protections for individuals and minorities are in real tension, not just under strain from bad actors, and that today's populism is simply democracy attacking liberalism as Mill once feared. His proposed fix borrows from Confucian political thought: a hybrid system blending meritocratic selection with limited democratic participation, rather than one-person-one-vote.

philosophy.headline: Four Islamic Polymaths Prove Breadth Beats Specialisation
philosophy.blurb: Aeon profiles al-Biruni, Alhazen, Avicenna and al-Khwarizmi, four scholars who moved freely between mathematics, medicine, astronomy and philosophy despite living under wildly different circumstances, from house arrest to court patronage. Their shared habit of testing one discipline's assumptions against another's, the essay argues, produced breakthroughs that narrower specialists of their eras could not have reached alone.

philosophy_101.text: A political model that selects some or all leaders by demonstrated ability and virtue rather than by popular vote, often proposed as a complement to or replacement for one-person-one-vote democracy.

The practice of working seriously across multiple, seemingly unrelated fields rather than specializing in one — a habit several of history's most original thinkers shared, and one modern academic specialization tends to discourage.
